rows.question: Does the technical documentation of a high-risk AI system require to provide specifications regarding the required hardware?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 11, a provider must draw up technical documentation containing the information set out in Annex IV, which expressly requires a description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run (Annex IV point 1(e)) and, as part of the system's development description, the computational resources used to develop, train, test and validate it (Annex IV point 2(c)).

rows.question: I have a medical device that has an AI system as a safety component. The medical device is classified "medium-risk" and undergoes a 3rd party conformity assessment. Is the AI system "medium risk" too? If yes, why? If not, why not?
rows.answer: No. The AI system is high-risk, not "medium-risk", Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 contains no "medium-risk" class for AI systems, and the risk class assigned to the device under the Medical Device Regulation does not carry across to the AI system. Classification runs through Article 6(1), which is binary and satisfied here on both of its cumulative limbs: point (a), the AI system is intended to be used as a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices is Annex I, point 11 (Section A); and point (b), that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment with a view to its placing on the market or putting into service under that legislation, which is exactly what the operator's device does. Article 6(1) applies irrespective of whether the AI system is placed on the market or put into service independently of the device. Where both limbs are met the system "shall be considered to be high-risk", the provision admits of no intermediate tier and no scaling of the AI classification to the sectoral device class; the device's MDR classification is legally relevant only insofar as it is what triggers the notified-body requirement in point (b). The Article 6(3) derogation, narrow procedural task, improvement of a previously completed human activity, detection of decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing human assessment, or a preparatory task, and in every case subject to the carve-out that profiling of natural persons is always high-risk, is unavailable to you: it derogates only from Article 6(2), the Annex III listed-use route, and the operator's system is classified under the Annex I product route. The documented self-assessment and Article 49(2) registration in Article 6(4) likewise concern only Annex III systems. The practical consequences are that the system must meet the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements pursuant to Article 8(1), including the documented, iterative lifecycle risk-management system of Article 9 (identification and analysis of known and reasonably foreseeable risks, estimation and evaluation of risks under intended purpose and reasonably foreseeable misuse, evaluation of post-market monitoring data, and targeted risk-management measures, with due consideration under Article 9(4) to the combined interaction of the requirements, testing under Article 9(5), and acceptable residual risks communicated to the deployer under Article 9(6)), the data-governance duties of Article 10 and the transparency and instructions-for-use duties of and that, under Article 43(3), you do not run a separate AI Act conformity assessment: the Section 2 requirements become part of the operator's existing MDR third-party procedure, controlled by the notified body notified under the MDR, with points 4.3, 4.4, 4.5 and the fifth paragraph of point 4.6 of Annex VII additionally applying (notified-body examination of the Annex IV technical documentation, access to training, validation and testing datasets, power to require further evidence or tests, and reasoned access to the training and trained models where other means are exhausted). Article 8(2) lets you integrate the AI Act testing, reporting, information and documentation into the MDR documentation and procedures you already maintain, and Article 43(4) requires a fresh assessment on substantial modification, save for changes to a continuously learning system that were pre-determined at the initial assessment and recorded in the technical documentation under point 2(f) of Annex IV. Neither Annex VI internal control nor a standalone Annex VII procedure is open to you, since both are routes for Annex III systems. In practice this aligns with the ISO 14971 hazard-identification and risk-evaluation cycle and the ISO 13485 design-control and traceability framework you already operate for the device.

Condition (a): AI system is safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation (medical devices under Regulation (EU) 2017/745)
Condition (b): that product is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment
Both conditions cumulative under Article 6(1), irrespective of the device's own sectoral risk classification

rows.question: We want to deploy an AI system that performs biometric verification solely to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be. Is this system prohibited? Is it high-risk?
rows.answer: No, the system is not a prohibited practice, and no, it is not high-risk on the biometrics route. On prohibition, none of the eight practices listed exhaustively in Article 5(1) captures one-to-one biometric verification. Point (h) bites only on the use of "real-time" remote biometric identification systems in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes, and then only outside its three permitted grounds in points (h)(i), (iii) (targeted search for victims of abduction, trafficking or sexual exploitation and search for missing persons; prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or physical safety or of a genuine and present or foreseeable terrorist attack; localisation or identification of a suspect for an Annex II offence punishable by at least four years' custody), whereas verification against a claimed identity is neither remote nor an identification practice. Point (g) prohibits biometric categorisation deducing race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation (save lawful labelling or filtering of lawfully acquired biometric datasets and categorisation of biometric data in law enforcement); points (a), (f) concern subliminal, manipulative or deceptive techniques, exploitation of vulnerabilities of age, disability or social or economic situation, social scoring, individual criminal-offence risk prediction by profiling or personality traits, untargeted facial-image scraping and emotion inference in the workplace and education. Mere confirmation that a person is who he or she claims to be engages none of them. On classification, Annex III, point 1(a) lists remote biometric identification systems but states expressly that this "shall not include AI systems intended to be used for biometric verification the sole purpose of which is to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be". The system therefore falls outside the Annex III listed use case altogether, and you never reach the Article 6(3) derogation or its conditions in points (a), (d) and the profiling proviso, because those presuppose a system "referred to in Annex III". The exclusion is conditioned on sole purpose: if the same system also performs one-to-many identification, biometric categorisation by sensitive or protected attributes (Annex III, point 1(b)) or emotion recognition (Annex III, point 1(c)), the carve-out is lost, and Annex III, point 1 applies in any event only in so far as the use is permitted under relevant Union or national law. Two residual routes remain open and must be checked separately. First, Article 6(1): the system is high-risk irrespective of Annex III if it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I (points 1 to 20) and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment under that legislation. Second, Article 6(2) with the remaining Annex III areas: verification embedded in a listed use case in another area, for example employment and worker management under Annex III, point 4(a) or (b), or migration, asylum and border control under Annex III, point 7, is high-risk by virtue of that other use case, not of point 1(a). Otherwise the system is non-high-risk, subject to Article 50(1), under which providers must ensure that AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed so that those persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless that is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person in the circumstances and context of use, and which does not apply to systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences with appropriate safeguards, unless available for the public to report an offence. Article 50(3) is not engaged, since it addresses deployers of emotion recognition and biometric categorisation systems only, and Article 4 AI literacy applies regardless of risk class.

Falls within Annex III.1(a) biometric verification exclusion

rows.question: Which article of the EU AI Act governs human oversight measures?
rows.answer: Human oversight of high-risk AI systems is governed by Article 14 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. Article 14(1) requires high-risk AI systems to be designed and developed, including with appropriate human-machine interface tools, so that they can be effectively overseen by natural persons while in use. Article 14(2) sets the objective: preventing or minimising risks to health, safety or fundamental rights arising from use in accordance with the intended purpose or under reasonably foreseeable misuse, in particular where such risks persist despite the other requirements of that Section. Under Article 14(3), the oversight measures must be commensurate with the risks, level of autonomy and context of use, and are ensured through either or both of: (a) measures identified and built into the system by the provider, when technically feasible, before it is placed on the market or put into service; and (b) measures identified by the provider before placing on the market or putting into service that are appropriate for implementation by the deployer. Article 14(4) requires that the system be provided to the deployer so that the natural persons assigned human oversight are enabled, as appropriate and proportionate, to: (a) properly understand the system's relevant capacities and limitations and duly monitor its operation, including detecting and addressing anomalies, dysfunctions and unexpected performance; (b) remain aware of the possible tendency to automatically rely or over-rely on the output (automation bias), in particular where the system provides information or recommendations for decisions taken by natural persons; (c) correctly interpret the system's output, taking into account the available interpretation tools and methods; (d) decide, in any particular situation, not to use the system or to otherwise disregard, override or reverse its output; and (e) intervene in the system's operation or interrupt it through a 'stop' button or similar procedure allowing the system to halt in a safe state. Article 14(5) adds a specific safeguard for the remote biometric identification systems referred to in point 1(a) of Annex III: the paragraph 3 measures must ensure that no action or decision is taken by the deployer on the basis of the identification resulting from the system unless that identification has been separately verified and confirmed by at least two natural persons with the necessary competence, training and authority. That two-person verification requirement does not apply to high-risk AI systems used for law enforcement, migration, border control or asylum purposes where Union or national law considers its application disproportionate.

rows.question: Under what conditions should providers of general-purpose AI models be subject to exceptions regarding transparency-related requirements, if any? And what do those exceptions not cover?
rows.answer: The exceptions to the GPAI transparency-related obligations are set out in Article 53(2). The Article 53(1)(a) duty to draw up and keep up-to-date the technical documentation of the model (Annex XI) and the Article 53(1)(b) duty to provide information and documentation to downstream providers (Annex XII) do not apply to providers that release the model under a free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification and distribution, where the model parameters, including the weights, and information on the model architecture and usage, are made publicly available. The exception does not cover the remaining Article 53(1) obligations: the policy to comply with Union copyright law (Article 53(1)(c)) and the publicly available, sufficiently detailed summary of the training content (Article 53(1)(d)) apply regardless of the licence. The exception also does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk (Article 53(2), second subparagraph), which remain subject to the full Article 53 obligations together with the Article 55 systemic-risk duties.

rows.question: What are the administrative fines for non-compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices?
rows.answer: Non-compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices in Article 5 attracts the Regulation's highest penalty tier: administrative fines of up to EUR 35 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 7 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher (Article 99(3)). This ceiling applies to any of the practices prohibited by Article 5(1), namely subliminal, manipulative or deceptive techniques materially distorting behaviour and causing significant harm (point (a)); exploitation of vulnerabilities due to age, disability or a specific social or economic situation (point (b)); social scoring leading to detrimental treatment in unrelated contexts or disproportionate to the social behaviour (point (c)); criminal-risk assessment based solely on profiling or personality traits (point (d)); untargeted scraping of facial images to build facial-recognition databases (point (e)); emotion inference in the workplace and in education institutions (point (f)); biometric categorisation deducing race, political opinions, trade-union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation (point (g)); and real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes outside the exhaustive derogations (point (h)). Two qualifiers attach to that ceiling. Where the offender is an SME, including a start-up, the fine is capped at the lower, not the higher, of the percentage and the fixed amount (Article 99(6)). And the amount actually imposed must, in each individual case, be effective, proportionate and dissuasive, taking into account the circumstances listed in Article 99(7): the nature, gravity and duration of the infringement and of its consequences, having regard to the purpose of the AI system and, where appropriate, the number of affected persons and the level of damage suffered by them; whether administrative fines have already been applied by other market surveillance authorities to the same operator for the same infringement; whether administrative fines have already been applied by other authorities to the same operator for infringements of other Union or national law, where such infringements result from the same activity or omission; the size, annual turnover and market share of the operator; any other aggravating or mitigating factor applicable to the circumstances of the case, such as financial benefits gained or losses avoided, directly or indirectly, from the infringement; the degree of cooperation with the national competent authorities to remedy the infringement and mitigate its possible adverse effects; the degree of responsibility of the operator, taking into account the technical and organisational measures implemented by it; the manner in which the infringement became known to the national competent authorities, in particular whether and to what extent the operator notified it; the intentional or negligent character of the infringement; and any action taken by the operator to mitigate the harm suffered by the affected persons. The remaining tiers are lower and do not apply to Article 5 breaches: up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3 % of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, for the operator and notified-body obligations listed exhaustively in Article 99(4)(a) to (g); and up to EUR 7 500 000 or 1 %, whichever is higher, for supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information to notified bodies or national competent authorities (Article 99(5)). Member States lay down the rules on penalties and notify them to the Commission (Article 99(1) and (2)), including the rules on whether and to what extent administrative fines may be imposed on public authorities and bodies established in their territory (Article 99(8)).

rows.question: What are all the risk categories in the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: The EU AI Act sets four risk tiers plus a separate regime for general-purpose AI models: unacceptable-risk practices are prohibited under Article 5; and high-risk systems are classified under Article 6 (an Annex I product safety component, or an Annex III use case) and carry the Chapter III Section 2 obligations. Limited-risk systems carry the Article 50 transparency duties, minimal-risk systems avoid Chapter III high-risk requirements but retain Article 4 AI literacy duties, with voluntary codes under Article 95, and general-purpose AI models are governed separately under Articles 51 to 56, with added obligations under Article 55 for models classified as having systemic risk under Article 51.

rows.question: Can an operator that is not a provider according to the EU AI Act, for example a deployer, take actions on a given high-risk AI system such that it can be effectively seen as a provider by the authorities? If yes, what kind of action would result in such an outcome?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 25(1), a distributor, importer, deployer or other third party is deemed to be the provider of a high-risk AI system, and takes on the provider obligations in Article 16, in any of three cases. First, if it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market (Article 25(1)(a)). Second, if it makes a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system that remains high-risk (Article 25(1)(b)). Third, if it modifies the intended purpose of an AI system, including a general-purpose AI system, so that it becomes high-risk (Article 25(1)(c)). In each of these three cases the operator assumes the provider obligations in Article 16, and the initial provider is no longer considered the provider of that specific system under Article 25(2).

rows.question: According to Article 1, what is the objective of the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: The objective of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 is to improve the functioning of the internal market and to promote the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy artificial intelligence, while ensuring a high level of protection of health, safety and the fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter, including democracy, the rule of law and environmental protection, against the harmful effects of AI systems in the Union, and supporting innovation (Article 1(1)). To that end, the Regulation lays down: harmonised rules for the placing on the market, the putting into service and the use of AI systems in the Union; prohibitions of certain AI practices; specific requirements for high-risk AI systems and obligations for operators of such systems; harmonised transparency rules for certain AI systems; harmonised rules for the placing on the market of general-purpose AI models; rules on market monitoring, market surveillance, governance and enforcement; and measures to support innovation, with a particular focus on SMEs, including start-ups (Article 1(2)(a), (g)).

rows.question: Is an AI system used to structure or deduplicate information for a use case listed in Annex III considered high-risk?
rows.answer: No. Structuring or deduplicating information is a narrow procedural task, so the system falls under the Article 6(3) first subparagraph point (a) derogation and is not high-risk, provided it poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights and does not materially influence the outcome of decision making; the other limbs are (b) improving the result of a previously completed human activity, (c) detecting decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment, and (d) performing a preparatory task, and the derogation never applies where the system profiles natural persons. Under Article 6(4) a provider relying on the derogation must document the assessment before the system is placed on the market or put into service, and register it under Article 49(2).

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what jurisdiction does the Court of Justice of the European Union have over Commission decisions fixing fines on providers of general-purpose AI models, and what can the Court do with the fine?
rows.answer: The Court of Justice of the European Union has unlimited jurisdiction to review Commission decisions fixing a fine on providers of general-purpose AI models, and in exercising it the Court may cancel, reduce or increase the fine imposed (Article 101(5)). "Unlimited jurisdiction" goes beyond ordinary annulment review of legality: the Court may substitute its own assessment of the amount for the Commission's, including upward, so a provider challenging a fine bears the risk that the fine is raised rather than merely annulled or lowered. That review attaches to decisions taken under Article 101(1), by which the Commission may fine a GPAI provider up to 3 % of its annual total worldwide turnover in the preceding financial year or EUR 15 000 000, whichever is higher, where it finds the provider intentionally or negligently (a) infringed the relevant provisions of the Regulation, (b) failed to comply with a request for a document or for information pursuant to Article 91 or supplied incorrect, incomplete or misleading information, (c) failed to comply with a measure requested under Article 93, or (d) failed to make available to the Commission access to the general-purpose AI model or general-purpose AI model with systemic risk with a view to an evaluation pursuant to Article 92. The substantive yardsticks the Court applies in re-fixing the amount are those binding on the Commission itself: regard to the nature, gravity and duration of the infringement, with due account of the principles of proportionality and appropriateness, and account taken of commitments made under Article 93(3) or in relevant codes of practice under Article 56 (Article 101(1)), together with the requirement that fines be effective, proportionate and dissuasive (Article 101(3)). Procedurally, the decision under review must have been preceded by communication of the Commission's preliminary findings to the provider and an opportunity to be heard (Article 101(2)), with detailed arrangements and procedural safeguards laid down in implementing acts adopted under the Article 98(2) examination procedure (Article 101(6)); defects in those safeguards are themselves reviewable grounds.

rows.question: When registering a high-risk AI system in the EU database under the EU AI Act, what specific information must the provider submit? List the required items.
rows.answer: A provider (or, where applicable, its authorised representative) registering itself and its Annex III high-risk AI system in the EU database before placing that system on the market or putting it into service (Article 49(1)) must enter the data listed in Section A of Annex VIII (Article 71(2)), namely: (1) the name, address and contact details of the provider; (2) where submission is carried out by another person on behalf of the provider, the name, address and contact details of that person; (3) the name, address and contact details of the authorised representative, where applicable; (4) the AI system trade name and any additional unambiguous reference allowing identification and traceability of the system; (5) a description of the intended purpose of the AI system and of the components and functions supported through it; (6) a basic and concise description of the information used by the system (data, inputs) and its operating logic; (7) the status of the AI system (on the market, or in service; no longer placed on the market/in service, recalled); (8) the type, number and expiry date of the certificate issued by the notified body and the name or identification number of that notified body, where applicable; (9) a scanned copy of that certificate, where applicable; (10) any Member States in which the system has been placed on the market, put into service or made available in the Union; (11) a copy of the EU declaration of conformity; (12) electronic instructions for use; and (13) a URL for additional information, which is optional. The registration must also identify the natural person responsible for registering the system who has legal authority to represent the provider (Article 71(5)). Three qualifications apply. First, point 12 (electronic instructions for use) is expressly not to be provided for high-risk systems in the areas of law enforcement or migration, asylum and border control management referred to in Annex III, points 1, 6 and 7 (Annex VIII, point 12). Second, for those same systems the registration is made in a secure non-public section of the database and is limited to Section A, points 1 to 10, with the exception of points 6, 8 and 9 (Article 49(4)(a)), access being confined to the Commission and the national authorities referred to in Article 74(8). Third, high-risk systems listed in point 2 of Annex III are excluded from EU-database registration and are registered at national level instead (Articles 49(1) and 49(5)). Where the provider has instead concluded under Article 6(3) that an Annex III system is not high-risk, it must still register itself and that system before placing it on the market, using Section B of Annex VIII (Articles 6(4) and 49(2)); Section C is populated separately by deployers that are public authorities, Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies (Article 49(3), Article 71(3)).

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, when a high-risk AI system is found to conform with the requirements, what information must the Union technical documentation assessment certificate contain?
rows.answer: Under Annex VII point 4.6, where the notified body finds the high-risk AI system conforms with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements, it issues a Union technical documentation assessment certificate. Per Annex VII point 4.6, that certificate must indicate the name and address of the provider, the conclusions of the examination, the conditions (if any) for its validity, and the data necessary for the identification of the AI system. Under Article 44(1) the certificate must be drawn up in a language which can be easily understood by the relevant authorities in the Member State in which the notified body is established, and under Article 44(2) it is valid for the period it indicates, which may not exceed five years for AI systems covered by Annex I and four years for AI systems covered by Annex III.

rows.question: Under Article 10(5) of the EU AI Act, when may a provider of a high-risk AI system process special categories of personal data for bias detection and correction, and what key safeguards/conditions must be met?
rows.answer: Under Article 10(5), a provider of a high-risk AI system may exceptionally process special categories of personal data only to the extent strictly necessary to ensure bias detection and correction, subject to appropriate safeguards. These conditions apply in addition to, and not instead of, Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 and Directive (EU) 2016/680. Article 10(5) requires all of the following: the bias work cannot be done with other data, including synthetic or anonymised data (a); technical limits on re-use plus state-of-the-art security and pseudonymisation (b); strict controls and documentation of access so that only authorised persons under appropriate confidentiality obligations can reach the data (c); the data are not transmitted, transferred or otherwise accessed by other parties (d); deletion once the bias is corrected or the retention period ends, whichever is first (e); and records of processing documenting why it was strictly necessary (f).

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what must a provider of a high-risk AI system supply to the deployer in the instructions for use? List the required categories of information.
rows.answer: A provider of a high‑risk AI system must accompany it with instructions for use in an appropriate digital format or otherwise, containing concise, complete, correct and clear information that is relevant, accessible and comprehensible to deployers (Article 13(2)), and that information must cover the following categories (Article 13(3)). First, the identity and contact details of the provider and, where applicable, of its authorised representative (Article 13(3)(a)). Second, the characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance of the system (Article 13(3)(b)), comprising its intended purpose; the level of accuracy, including its metrics, robustness and cybersecurity referred to in Article 15 against which the system has been tested and validated and which can be expected, together with any known or foreseeable circumstances that may affect that expected level (a declaration mirrored in Article 15(3)); any known or foreseeable circumstance, related to use in accordance with the intended purpose or under conditions of reasonably foreseeable misuse, that may lead to risks to health and safety or fundamental rights referred to in Article 9(2); where applicable, the technical capabilities and characteristics of the system to provide information relevant to explaining its output; when appropriate, its performance regarding specific persons or groups of persons on which the system is intended to be used; when appropriate, specifications for the input data or other relevant information on the training, validation and testing data sets used, having regard to the intended purpose; and, where applicable, information enabling deployers to interpret the output and use it appropriately. Third, the changes to the system and its performance that were pre‑determined by the provider at the moment of the initial conformity assessment, if any (Article 13(3)(c)). Fourth, the human oversight measures referred to in Article 14, including the technical measures put in place to facilitate deployers' interpretation of the system's outputs (Article 13(3)(d)). Fifth, the computational and hardware resources needed, the expected lifetime of the system, and any necessary maintenance and care measures, including their frequency, to ensure proper functioning, including as regards software updates (Article 13(3)(e)). Sixth, where relevant, a description of the mechanisms included within the system that allow deployers properly to collect, store and interpret the logs in accordance with Article 12 (Article 13(3)(f)). These instructions are the vehicle through which the risk‑management system discharges its residual‑risk information duty towards deployers under Article 9(5)(c), and they must be drawn up in a form meeting the accessibility requirements applicable under Article 16(1)(l).

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) Article 95, who may draw up codes of conduct, and which bodies must encourage and facilitate their drawing up?
rows.answer: Codes of conduct may be drawn up by individual providers or deployers of AI systems, by organisations representing them, or by both, and may be drawn up with the involvement of any interested stakeholders and their representative organisations, including civil society organisations and academia; a single code may cover one or more AI systems, taking into account the similarity of the intended purpose of the relevant systems (Article 95(3)). The bodies that must encourage and facilitate their drawing up are the AI Office and the Member States. Under Article 95(1) they shall encourage and facilitate the drawing up of codes of conduct, including related governance mechanisms, intended to foster the voluntary application to AI systems other than high-risk AI systems of some or all of the requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2, taking into account available technical solutions and industry best practices. Under Article 95(2) they shall also facilitate the drawing up of codes of conduct concerning the voluntary application, including by deployers, of specific requirements to all AI systems, on the basis of clear objectives and key performance indicators to measure the achievement of those objectives, including elements such as: applicable elements provided for in Union ethical guidelines for trustworthy AI; assessing and minimising the impact of AI systems on environmental sustainability, including energy-efficient programming and techniques for efficient design, training and use of AI; promoting AI literacy, in particular of persons dealing with the development, operation and use of AI; facilitating an inclusive and diverse design of AI systems, including through inclusive and diverse development teams and the promotion of stakeholders' participation; and assessing and preventing the negative impact of AI systems on vulnerable persons or groups of vulnerable persons, including as regards accessibility for persons with a disability, as well as on gender equality. When encouraging and facilitating the drawing up of codes of conduct, the AI Office and the Member States must take into account the specific interests and needs of SMEs, including start-ups (Article 95(4)).

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what minimum elements must a provider's quality management system (QMS) for high-risk AI systems include? List the required elements.
rows.answer: Under Article 17(1) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, a provider of a high-risk AI system must put in place a quality management system that ensures compliance with the Regulation and is documented in a systematic and orderly manner in the form of written policies, procedures and instructions. That system must include at least the following thirteen aspects: (a) a strategy for regulatory compliance, including compliance with conformity assessment procedures and procedures for the management of modifications to the high-risk AI system; (b) techniques, procedures and systematic actions for the design, design control and design verification of the system; (c) techniques, procedures and systematic actions for the development, quality control and quality assurance of the system; (d) examination, test and validation procedures to be carried out before, during and after development, and the frequency with which they are to be carried out; (e) technical specifications, including standards, to be applied and, where harmonised standards are not applied in full or do not cover all relevant requirements of Chapter III, Section 2, the means used to ensure compliance with those requirements; (f) systems and procedures for data management, including data acquisition, collection, analysis, labelling, storage, filtration, mining, aggregation, retention and any other data operation performed before and for the purpose of placing on the market or putting into service; (g) the risk management system referred to in Article 9; (h) the setting-up, implementation and maintenance of a post-market monitoring system in accordance with Article 72; (i) procedures related to the reporting of a serious incident in accordance with Article 73; (j) the handling of communication with national competent authorities, other relevant authorities including those providing or supporting access to data, notified bodies, other operators, customers or other interested parties; (k) systems and procedures for record-keeping of all relevant documentation and information; (l) resource management, including security-of-supply related measures; and (m) an accountability framework setting out the responsibilities of management and other staff with regard to all of those aspects. Implementation of these aspects must be proportionate to the size of the provider's organisation, but the provider must in any event respect the degree of rigour and level of protection required to ensure its high-risk AI systems comply with the Regulation (Article 17(2)). Providers already subject to quality management system obligations or an equivalent function under relevant sectoral Union law may incorporate the Article 17(1) aspects into that existing system (Article 17(3)). For providers that are financial institutions subject to internal governance, arrangements or processes requirements under Union financial services law, the obligation to put a quality management system in place is deemed fulfilled by complying with those internal governance rules, with the exception of points (g), (h) and (i) of Article 17(1), which continue to apply; harmonised standards referred to in Article 40 are to be taken into account for that purpose (Article 17(4)).

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, in which specific situations may law enforcement use 'real-time' remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes (i.e., the exceptions to the prohibition)? List the permitted objectives.
rows.answer: Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the prohibition in Article 5(1)(h) is disapplied only where the use of a 'real-time' remote biometric identification system in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes is strictly necessary for one of three exhaustively listed objectives: first, the targeted search for specific victims of abduction, trafficking in human beings or sexual exploitation of human beings, as well as the search for missing persons (Article 5(1)(h)(i)); second, the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to the life or physical safety of natural persons, or of a genuine and present or genuine and foreseeable threat of a terrorist attack (Article 5(1)(h)(ii)); and third, the localisation or identification of a person suspected of having committed a criminal offence, for the purpose of conducting a criminal investigation or prosecution or executing a criminal penalty, for offences referred to in Annex II and punishable in the Member State concerned by a custodial sentence or detention order for a maximum period of at least four years (Article 5(1)(h)(iii)). Annex II fixes that offence list, terrorism, trafficking in human beings, sexual exploitation of children and child sexual abuse material, illicit trafficking in narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances, illicit trafficking in weapons, munitions or explosives, murder, grievous bodily injury, illicit trade in human organs, illicit trafficking in nuclear or radioactive materials, kidnapping, illegal restraint and hostage-taking, crimes within the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Court, unlawful seizure of aircraft or ships, rape, environmental crime, organised or armed robbery, sabotage, and participation in a criminal organisation involved in one or more of those offences. Point (h) is without prejudice to Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 for the processing of biometric data for purposes other than law enforcement. These objectives are permissive only in combination with the conditions attached to them. Under Article 5(2), the system may be deployed solely to confirm the identity of the specifically targeted individual, and the deploying authority must take into account the nature of the situation giving rise to the possible use, in particular the seriousness, probability and scale of the harm that would be caused if the system were not used, and the consequences of the use for the rights and freedoms of all persons concerned, in particular the seriousness, probability and scale of those consequences; the use must also comply with necessary and proportionate safeguards and conditions under the national law authorising it, in particular as regards temporal, geographic and personal limitations, and is authorised only if the law-enforcement authority has completed a fundamental rights impact assessment under Article 27 and registered the system in the EU database under Article 49, save that in duly justified cases of urgency use may begin before registration provided registration follows without undue delay. Under Article 5(3), each use is further subject to prior authorisation by a judicial authority or an independent administrative authority whose decision is binding, granted on reasoned request; in a duly justified situation of urgency the use may be started without authorisation, but the authorisation must be requested without undue delay and at the latest within 24 hours, and if it is refused the use must be stopped immediately and all data, results and output discarded. Article 5(4) requires notification of each use to the relevant market surveillance authority and the national data protection authority, and Article 5(5) makes the whole derogation conditional on a Member State having chosen to provide, in its national law, for the possibility of authorising such use in full or in part within the limits of Article 5(1)(h) and Article 5(2) and (3). Absent such national implementing law, the derogation is unavailable and the practice remains prohibited in that Member State.

Prevention of specific, substantial and imminent threat to life/physical safety, or genuine terrorist attack threat

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what must providers of AI systems that generate or manipulate synthetic content do to enable identification of AI-generated/manipulated output, and what quality criteria must that solution meet?
rows.answer: Providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, that generate synthetic audio, image, video or text content must ensure that the outputs of the system are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated (Article 50(2)). The duty attaches at the design and provision stage, so the marking must be built into the system's outputs rather than left to the deployer, and it applies to all four content modalities. The technical solution used to achieve that marking must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable, but only as far as this is technically feasible, taking into account the specificities and limitations of the various types of content, the costs of implementation and the generally acknowledged state of the art, as may be reflected in relevant technical standards (Article 50(2)). This is therefore a proportionate, state-of-the-art benchmark rather than an absolute guarantee of indelible marking, and compliance is assessed against what the acknowledged state of the art for the relevant content type permits at the time. The obligation is subject to three carve-outs (Article 50(2)): it does not apply to the extent that the AI system performs an assistive function for standard editing; it does not apply to the extent that the system does not substantially alter the input data provided by the deployer or the semantics thereof; and it does not apply where the system is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences. Where marking information is provided to natural persons, it must be given in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of the first interaction or exposure, and must conform to the applicable accessibility requirements (Article 50(5)). The Article 50(2) duty operates without prejudice to the Chapter III requirements and to other transparency obligations under Union or national law (Article 50(6)), and the AI Office is to encourage and facilitate codes of practice at Union level to facilitate effective implementation of the detection and labelling obligations, which the Commission may approve by implementing act under the Article 56(6) procedure or, if it considers a code inadequate, replace with common rules specified by implementing act under the Article 98(2) examination procedure (Article 50(7)). Separate from the provider's machine-readable marking duty, the deployer of an AI system that generates or manipulates image, audio or video content constituting a deep fake must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated; this does not apply where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, and where the content forms part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous work or programme the obligation is limited to disclosing the existence of such generated or manipulated content in an appropriate manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work (Article 50(4)).

Exemptions: assistive editing, no substantial alteration of input data/semantics, or law-enforcement authorisation

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, which body has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce the obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models (Chapter V), and which entity is entrusted with implementing those tasks?
rows.answer: The Commission holds exclusive powers to supervise and enforce Chapter V, the obligations of providers of general-purpose AI models, and it must entrust the implementation of those tasks to the AI Office (Article 88(1)). That exclusivity is qualified in three ways on the face of the provision: the Commission must take into account the procedural guarantees under Article 94; the entrustment to the AI Office is without prejudice to the Commission's own powers of organisation; and it is likewise without prejudice to the division of competences between the Member States and the Union based on the Treaties (Article 88(1)). Complementing this, and without prejudice to Article 75(3), market surveillance authorities may request the Commission to exercise the powers laid down in that Section where doing so is necessary and proportionate to assist them in fulfilling their tasks under the Regulation (Article 88(2)), a request mechanism, not a transfer of enforcement competence over Chapter V. Providers of general-purpose AI models must in turn cooperate as necessary with the Commission and the national competent authorities in the exercise of their competences and powers under the Regulation (Article 53(3)).

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what conditions must be met before data collected and processed for testing high-risk AI systems in real-world conditions can be transferred to a third country (outside the EU)?
rows.answer: Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, data collected and processed for the purpose of testing a high-risk AI system in real world conditions may be transferred to a third country only provided that appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law are implemented (Article 60(4)(e)). That is the sole condition the Regulation itself attaches to the transfer: the Act does not create a bespoke transfer mechanism but conditions the transfer on compliance with the safeguards that Union law, in particular Union data protection law, already makes applicable to the data in question. This condition is cumulative, not alternative: it is one of the conditions in Article 60(4) that must all be met before a provider or prospective provider may conduct testing in real world conditions at all, alongside the submission and approval of the real-world testing plan by the market surveillance authority, registration of the testing, establishment or legal representation in the Union, and informed consent of the subjects of the testing.

rows.question: What are the conditions to classify general-purpose AI (GPAI) model as "GPAI model with systemic risk"? Do all need to be met at the same time?
rows.answer: No, the conditions are alternatives, not cumulative: Article 51(1) provides that a general-purpose AI model is classified as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk "if it meets any of the following conditions", so satisfying one limb is sufficient. The two limbs are: (a) it has high impact capabilities evaluated on the basis of appropriate technical tools and methodologies, including indicators and benchmarks; and (b) based on a decision of the Commission, taken ex officio or following a qualified alert from the scientific panel, it has capabilities or an impact equivalent to those referred to in point (a), having regard to the criteria set out in Annex XIII (Article 51(1)(a), (b)). Limb (a) is supported by a rebuttable presumption: a model is presumed to have high impact capabilities where the cumulative amount of computation used for its training, measured in floating-point operations, is greater than 10^25 (Article 51(2)). That is a presumption attached to limb (a) only, not a third independent condition, and the terms it relies on are defined in Article 3: "high-impact capabilities" as capabilities that match or exceed the capabilities recorded in the most advanced general-purpose AI models (Article 3(64)), "systemic risk" as a risk specific to such high-impact capabilities having a significant impact on the Union market due to reach or to actual or reasonably foreseeable negative effects on public health, safety, public security, fundamental rights or society as a whole, capable of propagating at scale across the value chain (Article 3(65)), and "floating-point operation" (Article 3(67)). The model must of course first qualify as a general-purpose AI model within Article 3(63). The Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts under Article 97 to amend the thresholds in Article 51(1) and (2) and to supplement the benchmarks and indicators in light of evolving technological developments, such as algorithmic improvements or increased hardware efficiency, where necessary for those thresholds to reflect the state of the art (Article 51(3)). The consequence of meeting either limb is that the provider owes the Article 55(1) obligations in addition to those in Articles 53 and 54, model evaluation under standardised protocols including documented adversarial testing; assessment and mitigation of possible systemic risks at Union level including their sources; tracking, documenting and reporting serious incidents and possible corrective measures without undue delay to the AI Office and, as appropriate, national competent authorities; and ensuring an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure (Article 55(1)(a), (d)). Classification as a model with systemic risk also removes the open-source exemption: the Article 53(1)(a) and (b) carve-out for models released under a free and open-source licence with publicly available parameters, weights, architecture and usage information does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risks (Article 53(2)).

Condition (b): Commission decision (ex officio or following qualified alert from scientific panel) that capabilities/impact are equivalent, per Annex XIII criteria
No, not cumulative - either condition alone suffices

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, is an AI system that is a safety component of a medical device classified as MDR Class I (non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable surgical) automatically a high-risk AI system? Explain your reasoning.
rows.answer: No. Such an AI system is not automatically a high-risk AI system under the Annex I product route. Article 6(1) makes an AI system high-risk only where both conditions are fulfilled cumulatively: (a) the AI system is intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or is itself a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I; and (b) that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment with a view to its placing on the market or putting into service pursuant to that Annex I legislation. Condition (a) is satisfied here, because Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices is listed in Annex I, point 11, and the AI system is a safety component of a device covered by it. Condition (b) is not satisfied: a Class I device that is non-sterile, has no measuring function and is not a reusable surgical instrument is the one MDR class for which the manufacturer self-declares conformity without notified body involvement, so no third-party conformity assessment is required for its placing on the market. With limb (b) unmet, Article 6(1) does not classify the system as high-risk. Classification is not thereby closed. Under Article 6(2), the system is still high-risk if it falls within a listed use case of in a medical context most plausibly Annex III, point 5(a) (evaluating eligibility of natural persons for essential public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare services, by or on behalf of public authorities) or point 5(d) (evaluating and classifying emergency calls, dispatching or prioritising emergency first response services, and emergency healthcare patient triage systems), and, for a system captured by Annex III, Article 6(3) permits a derogation only where it poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision-making, and one of four conditions applies: (a) a narrow procedural task; (b) improving the result of a previously completed human activity; (c) detecting decision-making patterns or deviations from prior patterns, without being meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment without proper human review; or (d) a preparatory task to an assessment relevant to an Annex III use case. That derogation never applies where the system performs profiling of natural persons, and a provider relying on it must document the assessment before placing the system on the market or putting it into service, is subject to the registration obligation in Article 49(2), and must supply that documentation to national competent authorities on request. A further caveat on the facts: if the intended purpose of the AI safety component itself changes the device's risk class under the MDR classification rules, for example by giving the device a measuring or active diagnostic function, the device would no longer sit in the self-certified Class I category, notified body involvement would be triggered, and Article 6(1)(b) would then be met.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, can an AI system intended to be used as a safety component in a lift qualify as a high-risk AI system, and under what conditions?
rows.answer: Yes. An AI system intended to be used as a safety component of a lift can be a high-risk AI system, under the Annex I product route in Article 6(1), and it qualifies only where both cumulative conditions of that paragraph are met: first, the AI system is intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or is itself a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in lifts and safety components for lifts are covered, because Annex I point 4 lists Directive 2014/33/EU on the harmonisation of the laws of the Member States relating to lifts and safety components for lifts; and second, the product whose safety component the AI system is, or the AI system itself as a product, is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment with a view to its placing on the market or putting into service pursuant to that Annex I legislation (Article 6(1), points (a) and (b)). Both limbs must be satisfied; a lift-related AI system that is not a safety component (or not itself such a product), or whose relevant product faces no third-party conformity assessment requirement under Directive 2014/33/EU, does not qualify on this route. Classification applies irrespective of whether the AI system is placed on the market or put into service independently of the lift or safety component in which it is integrated (Article 6(1)). The mitigation in Article 6(3) is not available here: it operates only by derogation from Article 6(2) for AI systems referred to in Annex III, and its conditions (narrow procedural task; improving the result of a previously completed human activity; detecting decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the previously completed human assessment absent proper human review; or performing a preparatory task), together with the profiling proviso and the documentation and registration duties in Article 6(4), have no application to the Annex I product route. A lift safety component can therefore reach high-risk status through Article 6(2) only if it independently falls within an Annex III use case. As to conformity assessment, because Directive 2014/33/EU is listed in Section A of Annex I, the provider follows the relevant conformity assessment procedure required under that Directive rather than the Annex VI internal-control or Annex VII procedures used for Annex III systems; the Chapter III Section 2 requirements apply to the system and form part of that assessment, and points 4.3, 4.4, 4.5 and the fifth paragraph of point 4.6 of Annex VII also apply (Article 43(3)). Notified bodies notified under Directive 2014/33/EU may control conformity with the Section 2 requirements provided their compliance with this Regulation's notified-body requirements has been assessed in the context of the notification procedure under that Directive, and where that Directive allows the product manufacturer to opt out of third-party conformity assessment on the basis of having applied all harmonised standards covering the relevant requirements, that option may be used only if the manufacturer has also applied harmonised standards or, where applicable, common specifications covering all Section 2 requirements (Article 43(3)). A new conformity assessment is required in the event of a substantial modification, regardless of whether the modified system is further distributed or continues to be used by the current deployer, while pre-determined changes for continuously learning systems that were fixed by the provider at the initial assessment and documented under point 2(f) of Annex IV do not constitute a substantial modification (Article 43(4)).

Both conditions cumulative

rows.question: A provider becomes aware of a risk (within the meaning of Article 79(1)) for their high-risk AI system. Does the provider need to take immediate corrective action OR immediately investigate the causes OR both? For example, perhaps it's the market surveillance authority that must investigate the cause, and the provider can help later.
rows.answer: Both, the two duties run in parallel and both are immediate; they are not sequenced, and neither is displaced by the market surveillance authority's own evaluation. Under Article 20(1), a provider that considers or has reason to consider that a high-risk AI system it has placed on the market or put into service is not in conformity must immediately take the necessary corrective actions, bringing the system into conformity, withdrawing it, disabling it, or recalling it, as appropriate, and must inform the distributors and, where applicable, the deployers, the authorised representative and the importers. Under Article 20(2), where that system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1) and the provider becomes aware of that risk, it must immediately investigate the causes, in collaboration with the reporting deployer where applicable, and inform the market surveillance authorities competent for the system and, where applicable, the notified body that issued a certificate under Article 44, in particular of the nature of the non-compliance and of any relevant corrective action taken. The phrase "any relevant corrective action taken" in Article 20(2) presupposes that the Article 20(1) corrective action is already under way, confirming that investigation does not come first or instead. The operator's alternative reading is incorrect. The market surveillance authority's evaluation under Article 79(2) is a separate, additional layer of public enforcement, not a substitute for the provider's own causal investigation: it is triggered by the authority's own sufficient reason to consider that a system presents a risk, obliges it to assess compliance with all requirements and obligations of the Regulation, to give particular attention to risks to vulnerable groups, and, where fundamental-rights risks are identified, to inform and fully cooperate with the national public authorities or bodies referred to in Article 77(1). In that procedure the operator's role is to cooperate as necessary with the authority and those bodies, and, where non-compliance is found, to carry out the corrective actions the authority requires within the prescribed period (in any event within the shorter of 15 working days or the period set by the relevant Union harmonisation legislation), with Article 18 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 applying to those measures. Article 79(4) further requires the operator to ensure that all appropriate corrective action is taken in respect of all the AI systems concerned that it has made available on the Union market, and Article 79(5) empowers the authority to impose provisional prohibition, restriction, withdrawal or recall measures if the operator fails to act adequately, a consequence that only makes sense because the primary corrective duty rests on the provider. Where the same facts also constitute a serious incident, Article 73(6) reinforces this: after reporting under Article 73(1), the provider must without delay perform the necessary investigations into the incident and the system, including a risk assessment of the incident and corrective action, cooperating with the competent authorities and, where relevant, the notified body, and must not conduct any investigation involving alteration of the system in a way that may affect a subsequent evaluation of the causes before informing the competent authorities of that action.

Immediate investigation of causes is the provider's own duty under Article 20(2)
Investigation done in collaboration with reporting deployer where applicable, not deferred to market surveillance authority

rows.question: My local small language model says that, as a distributor of high-risk AI systems, I must be careful that transport conditions do not jeopardize compliance. But AI is just software, isn't it? So I am pretty sure my model hallucinated. What do you say?
rows.answer: The operator's model did not hallucinate: Article 24(3) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 states, in terms, that distributors shall ensure that, while a high-risk AI system is under their responsibility, storage or transport conditions, where applicable, do not jeopardise the compliance of the system with the requirements set out in Section 2. The premise that "AI is just software" is what fails here, and the Regulation anticipates that objection with the qualifier "where applicable". A high-risk AI system is frequently not delivered as a bare download: on the Annex I product route it is a safety component of, or is itself, a physical product subject to Union harmonisation legislation, and even on the Annex III listed-use route it may be embodied in hardware, sensors, or physical media that a distributor warehouses and ships. In those cases mishandling during storage or carriage, damaged sensors, corrupted media, missing or defaced CE marking, a lost paper copy of the EU declaration of conformity or the instructions for use, can genuinely degrade conformity with the Section 2 requirements. Where a system truly reaches the market only as an electronic transmission with no physical custody, the "where applicable" wording means the duty has no practical object, but it is not disapplied by a general claim that AI is immaterial. Two points on scope. The duty is limited to the period while the system is under the distributor's responsibility, so it does not extend to conditions before receipt or after onward supply. And it does not stand alone: before making the system available on the market the operator must verify under Article 24(1) that it bears the required CE marking, that it is accompanied by a copy of the EU declaration of conformity referred to in Article 47 and the instructions for use, and that the provider and importer, as applicable, have complied with Article 16, points (b) and (c) and Article 23(3). If you consider or have reason to consider, on the basis of the information in the operator's possession, that the system is not in conformity with Section 2, Article 24(2) bars you from making it available until it has been brought into conformity, and where it presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1) the operator must inform the provider or the importer. If the non-conformity concerns a system you have already made available, which is the likely posture if transport damage is discovered late, Article 24(4) requires the operator to take the corrective actions necessary to bring it into conformity, to withdraw it or recall it, or to ensure that the provider, the importer or any relevant operator takes those actions, and, where the system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), to inform the provider or importer and the competent authorities immediately with details of the non-compliance and of any corrective actions taken. Article 24(5) obliges you, upon a reasoned request from a relevant competent authority, to provide all information and documentation regarding the operator's actions under paragraphs 1 to 4 necessary to demonstrate conformity, and Article 24(6) requires cooperation with competent authorities in any action they take in relation to a high-risk AI system you made available, in particular to reduce or mitigate the risk it poses. In practice this means keeping handling and storage instructions from the provider, controlling warehouse and shipping conditions for any physical embodiment, and retaining records sufficient to show that compliance was not jeopardised while the system was in the operator's hands.

rows.question: Does the AI Act prohibit or classifies as high-risk the use of AI in drones? Can I use AI in a drone to find who's around in town? And what if it's just a toy drone? And what about toy drones used for other applications?
rows.answer: The system described is not among the practices prohibited under Article 5 (social scoring, untargeted facial-image scraping, manipulative or exploitative techniques, and the other exhaustively-listed bans). Whether it is high-risk turns on Article 6: it is high-risk only if it is a safety component of a product regulated under Annex I (for example a medical device under the MDR or IVDR) or falls within one of the Annex III use cases. Otherwise it is limited- or minimal-risk, subject mainly to the Article 50 transparency duties where it interacts directly with people.

Drone AI identifying people in public = remote biometric identification, high-risk under Annex III(1)(a), not the 1:1 verification exclusion
Toy status irrelevant — classification depends on intended use, not the device
Toy drone used for other application is high-risk only if that use matches Annex III (or Article 6(1) safety-component/conformity-assessment criteria)

rows.question: We deployed a high-risk AI system in our company. We have a use in mind that is outside the intended use and our legal team say such a use is definitely no risk (no Annex I nor III apply). Can we just go ahead with the new use and do we need to keep logs for it?
rows.answer: No, you cannot simply switch to the new use, and yes, the operator must keep the logs. As a deployer the operator is bound by Article 26(1) to take appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure you use the high-risk AI system in accordance with the instructions of use. A use the operator's own team describes as "outside the intended use" is by definition off-label, and Article 26(1) does not contain a carve-out for off-label uses that the deployer judges to be low-risk. The operator's legal team's conclusion answers a different question: Article 6 decides whether a system is high-risk, through the Annex I product route (Article 6(1): the system is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment) or the Annex III route (Article 6(2): the system falls within a lettered use-case under one of the eight Annex III areas). That classification attaches to the system as placed on the market on the basis of the provider's declared intended purpose; a deployer's later choice of a different use does not de-classify it. The Article 6(3) derogation cannot help you either: it applies only to Annex III systems, requires no significant risk of harm plus one of the four conditions (narrow procedural task; improving the result of a previously completed human activity; detecting decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the previously completed human assessment without proper human review; or a preparatory task), never applies where the system performs profiling of natural persons, and is a provider self-assessment that must be documented before the system is placed on the market, it is not a post-deployment route for a deployer. There is also a role risk. Under Article 25, a deployer that makes a substantial modification, puts its own name or trademark on the system, or modifies the intended purpose in a way that makes a system high-risk, becomes a provider and assumes the full provider obligations (Chapter III Section 2 compliance, quality management, technical documentation, conformity assessment, EU declaration of conformity, CE marking, registration, corrective action), with the initial provider owing you the information, technical access and assistance needed to meet them under Article 25(2). Conversely, if you stay within the existing system and merely use it differently, the correct route is to go back to the provider: the new use must be brought within the intended purpose and the instructions of use, with the risk-management system updated accordingly, since Article 9(2)(b) already requires the provider to estimate and evaluate risks arising both in intended use and under conditions of reasonably foreseeable misuse, and Article 9(6) requires testing that the system performs consistently for its intended purpose. On logging, the duty is unchanged by the fact that the use is new or claimed to be risk-free. Article 26(6) requires you, as deployer of a high-risk AI system, to keep the logs automatically generated by that system, to the extent those logs are under the operator's control, for at least six months, unless applicable Union or national law provides otherwise; the only carve-out is that deployers which are financial institutions subject to internal-governance requirements under Union financial-services law fulfil this obligation (and the Article 26(5) monitoring obligation) by complying with the governance arrangements under that law. The mirror-image provider duty in Article 19(1) is to keep the Article 12(1) logs under its control for a period appropriate to the intended purpose, of at least six months, without prejudice to Union or national law, in particular data-protection law. The operator must also continue to monitor operation on the basis of the instructions of use and inform the provider of serious incidents under Article 26(5), an obligation you cannot discharge coherently while operating outside those instructions, and, if this is a workplace deployment, inform workers' representatives and affected workers before putting the system into service under Article 26(7). The practical answer is therefore to obtain a provider-side extension of the intended purpose and updated instructions of use (or accept provider status under Article 25) before starting the new use, and to retain the automatically generated logs for at least six months throughout.

rows.question: Is AI software that helps clinicians take medical decisions around best treatment potentially high-risk? According to what Article and/or Annex?
rows.answer: Yes. AI software that supports clinicians in choosing the best treatment is potentially high-risk under the EU AI Act, and the principal route is Article 6(1) read with Annex I, not Annex III. Article 6(1) classifies an AI system as high-risk, irrespective of whether it is placed on the market or put into service independently of a product, where two cumulative conditions are met: (a) the AI system is intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or is itself a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I; and (b) that product, or the AI system as a product, is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment with a view to placing on the market or putting into service under that Annex I legislation. Clinical decision-support software with a medical purpose is normally a medical device within Regulation (EU) 2017/745 (Annex I, point 11) or, where it interprets results from in vitro examinations, Regulation (EU) 2017/746 (Annex I, point 12). Treatment-recommendation software of that kind is generally classified above the lowest risk class and therefore requires notified-body involvement, so both limbs of Article 6(1) are satisfied and the system is high-risk. Where the software is not a medical device, or falls in a device class that permits self-certification only, limb (b) fails and Article 6(1) does not bite. The Annex III route is narrower and does not cover clinical treatment decisions as such. It is engaged only where the system also fits a listed use, most relevantly Annex III, point 5(a), AI systems intended to be used by or on behalf of public authorities to evaluate the eligibility of natural persons for essential public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare services, and to grant, reduce, revoke or reclaim them, or point 5(d), covering emergency healthcare patient triage systems and the evaluation, classification and dispatch prioritisation of emergency calls and first-response services. Article 6(2) makes any Annex III system high-risk. The Article 6(3) derogation is available only for the Annex III route, never for an Annex I medical device. Under it, an Annex III system is not high-risk where it does not pose a significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision-making, and one of four conditions is met: (a) it performs a narrow procedural task; (b) it improves the result of a previously completed human activity; (c) it detects decision-making patterns or deviations from prior patterns and is not meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment without proper human review; or (d) it performs a preparatory task to an assessment relevant to an Annex III use case. Notwithstanding those conditions, the system is always high-risk where it performs profiling of natural persons. A treatment-recommendation tool that materially influences the clinician's choice will not qualify, since it goes beyond a preparatory or narrow procedural function. Independently of classification, Article 50(1) requires providers to ensure that an AI system intended to interact directly with natural persons, for example a patient-facing interface, is designed so that the person is informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless that is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person in the circumstances and context of use; the information must be given clearly and distinguishably at the latest at the time of first interaction and must conform to applicable accessibility requirements. The prohibitions in Article 5 are not engaged by ordinary clinical decision support. In practice the AI Act's requirements for such software are discharged alongside the medical device framework, with the risk management and data governance duties dovetailing with ISO 14971 and ISO 13485 practice.

Article 6(2)
Annex III (healthcare access/provision)
