rows.question: About obligations of transparency to providers who want to use a GPAI model, do you need to disclose: date of release? number of paramaters? applicable model interaction with hardware? license? samples of outlier data used in training? Given clear yes/no to each item.
rows.answer: Yes to the first four; no to the fifth. The duty owed to providers of AI systems that intend to integrate the model is Article 53(1)(b), which requires the provider to draw up, keep up to date and make available information and documentation that (i) enables those providers to understand the model's capabilities and limitations and to comply with their own obligations, and (ii) contains at a minimum the elements of Annex XII, all without prejudice to intellectual property rights and confidential business information or trade secrets. Date of release: yes, Annex XII.1(c) requires the date of release and methods of distribution. Number of parameters: yes, Annex XII.1(f) requires the architecture and number of parameters. Model interaction with hardware: yes, where applicable, Annex XII.1(d) requires how the model interacts, or can be used to interact, with hardware or software that is not part of the model itself; Annex XII.2(a) separately requires the technical means (e.g. instructions for use, infrastructure, tools) required for integration into AI systems. Licence: yes, Annex XII.1(h) requires the licence for the model. Samples of outlier data used in training: no. Annex XII.2(c) requires only information on the data used for training, testing and validation, where applicable, including the type and provenance of data and curation methodologies; it does not require data samples, and the reference to outlier detection as a data-cleaning methodology sits in Annex IV.2(d), which governs the technical documentation of high-risk AI systems, not the Annex XII downstream-provider package. For completeness, the remaining Annex XII elements are the tasks the model is intended to perform and the type and nature of AI systems into which it can be integrated (XII.1(a)), the acceptable use policies applicable (XII.1(b)), the versions of relevant software related to use of the model, where applicable (XII.1(e)), and the modality and format of inputs and outputs (XII.1(g)), with XII.2(b) adding the modality and format of inputs and outputs and their maximum size, such as context-window length. Two qualifications bound this. Under Article 53(2) the Article 53(1)(b) downstream-information obligation (like the Article 53(1)(a) Annex XI documentation obligation) does not apply to models released under a free and open-source licence allowing access, use, modification and distribution, with publicly available parameters including weights, information on model architecture and information on model use, but that exemption falls away for models classified as having systemic risk under Article 51. The Article 53(1)(c) copyright policy and the Article 53(1)(d) publicly available training-content summary apply regardless.

rows.question: Name the areas of high-risk use cases. Is healthcare decision making one of them?
rows.answer: Healthcare decision-making is not, as such, one of the areas of high-risk use cases; it is not an Annex III heading, though several healthcare-related use cases do fall within Annex III area 5 and certain medical AI is high-risk through the Annex I product route instead. Annex III lists eight areas, each a numbered heading under which only the lettered use-cases make a system high-risk under Article 6(2): biometrics (in so far as their use is permitted under Union or national law); critical infrastructure; education and vocational training; employment, workers' management and access to self-employment; access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits; law enforcement (in so far as permitted under Union or national law); migration, asylum and border control management; and administration of justice and democratic processes (Annex III, points 1 to 8). Healthcare surfaces inside area 5 rather than as an area of its own: AI systems intended to be used by or on behalf of public authorities to evaluate the eligibility of natural persons for essential public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare services, and to grant, reduce, revoke or reclaim them (Annex III, point 5(a)); AI systems for risk assessment and pricing in relation to natural persons in life and health insurance (Annex III, point 5(c)); and AI systems intended to evaluate and classify emergency calls or to dispatch or prioritise the dispatching of emergency first response services, including medical aid, as well as emergency healthcare patient triage systems (Annex III, point 5(d)). A health risk assessment concerning a person entering a Member State's territory falls instead under migration, asylum and border control (Annex III, point 7(b)). Clinical AI outside those listed uses is not high-risk by virtue of Annex III; it becomes high-risk under the separate product route where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in notably the Medical Devices Regulation (EU) 2017/745 and the In Vitro Diagnostic Medical Devices Regulation (EU) 2017/746 (Annex I, points 11 and 12), and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment (Article 6(1)(a) and (b)). Two qualifications complete the picture. A system caught by Annex III is nonetheless not high-risk where it poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision-making, and it performs a narrow procedural task, improves the result of a previously completed human activity, detects decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the previously completed human assessment absent proper human review, or performs a preparatory task, but it is always high-risk where it performs profiling of natural persons (Article 6(3)). And the areas themselves are closed: the Commission may amend Annex III only by adding or modifying use-cases within the areas already listed, and only where the systems also pose a risk of harm to health and safety, or an adverse impact on fundamental rights, equivalent to or greater than that of the systems already listed, both conditions being cumulative (Article 7(1)(a) and (b)).

rows.question: Could the introduction of guardrails in an AI agentic system reduce the risk of the system from high risk to moderate risk? What about changing the capabilities and intended use of the system?
rows.answer: No. Adding guardrails to an agentic system does not move it out of the high-risk class, because classification under Article 6 turns on what the system is and what it is intended to be used for, not on how well its risks are controlled. Under Article 6(1) a system is high-risk if it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by Annex I harmonisation legislation that must undergo third-party conformity assessment; under Article 6(2) it is high-risk if it falls within a listed use-case under one of the eight Annex III areas (biometrics; critical infrastructure; education and vocational training; employment and worker management; essential private and public services; law enforcement; migration, asylum and border control; administration of justice and democratic processes). Guardrails are risk-control measures, and Articles 8(1) and 9 place them downstream of classification: the Article 9 risk-management system, identifying known and foreseeable risks, estimating risks from reasonably foreseeable misuse, evaluating post-market monitoring data, and adopting targeted mitigation measures, is an obligation that follows from being high-risk, so deploying it cannot be the ground for ceasing to be high-risk. Nor is there a "moderate risk" legal category to descend into: Article 50 transparency duties attach to particular system types (direct interaction with natural persons, synthetic content generation, emotion recognition, biometric categorisation, deepfakes, public-interest text) independently of Article 6, and a system can owe both sets of duties at once. Guardrails are nevertheless legally relevant in three narrower ways. They are part of the characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance that must be described in the instructions for use under Article 13(3)(b), including the accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity levels tested against (13(3)(b)(ii)) and the circumstances, in intended use or reasonably foreseeable misuse, that may lead to risks to health, safety or fundamental rights (13(3)(b)(iii)); any guardrail-related changes pre-determined at the initial conformity assessment must be disclosed under Article 13(3)(c) if they are to be made without triggering a fresh assessment. They reduce residual risk under Article 9 and so affect whether the Chapter III Section 2 requirements are met, judged against the intended purpose and the generally acknowledged state of the art (Article 8(1)). And at the legislative level only, the availability of effective measures to prevent or substantially minimise risks, and of redress, is a criterion the Commission weighs under Article 7(2)(k)(i), (ii) when deciding whether to add or modify an Annex III use-case by delegated act, a power exercised by the Commission under Article 97, not by a provider over its own product. Changing capabilities and intended use is different, and can change the classification, in both directions. Because Article 6(2) operates on the listed use-case, restricting a system so that it is no longer intended for any Annex III use-case takes it outside the Annex III route altogether (the Annex I route must be tested separately, and is not escaped by narrowing intended purpose if the system remains a safety component of, or is, a product requiring third-party conformity assessment). Within Annex III, Article 6(3) derogates where the system poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision-making, and meets at least one of four conditions: it performs a narrow procedural task; it improves the result of a previously completed human activity; it detects decision-making patterns or deviations from prior decision-making patterns without replacing or influencing the previously completed human assessment without proper human review; or it performs a preparatory task to an assessment relevant to an Annex III use-case. That derogation is unavailable, the system is always high-risk, where it performs profiling of natural persons. The provider must document its assessment before the system is placed on the market or put into service, and such systems are still subject to registration under Article 49. This is where the distinction matters for an agentic system: a restriction only helps if it genuinely redefines what the system is intended and able to do, so that it fits one of the Article 6(3) limbs and does not materially influence decision outcomes. A guardrail bolted onto an agent that still autonomously screens candidates, allocates tasks, or evaluates performance leaves the system squarely within the Annex III employment and worker management use-cases; a design change that reduces the agent to a preparatory or narrow procedural step, with the substantive assessment made by a human, is a change of intended purpose and can engage Article 6(3). Removing a use-case from Annex III itself is reserved to the Commission under Article 7(3), on the cumulative conditions that the system no longer poses any significant risk to fundamental rights, health or safety in light of the Article 7(2) criteria, and that the deletion does not decrease the overall level of protection under Union law. Modification carries its own consequences. Under Article 25(1) a distributor, importer, deployer or other third party becomes a provider, subject to the Article 16 obligations, where it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk system already on the market (subject to contractual allocation), where it makes a substantial modification to a high-risk system such that it remains high-risk under Article 6, or where it modifies the intended purpose of a system, including a general-purpose AI system, not previously classified as high-risk so that it becomes high-risk. The Act provides no mirror-image provision by which a deployer's narrowing of intended purpose discharges the original provider; if the original system was placed on the market as high-risk for a stated intended purpose, the provider's Chapter III obligations attach to that placing, and the initial provider must in any event cooperate with a new provider under Article 25(2) by supplying the necessary information, technical access and assistance, in particular for conformity assessment. Finally, if the agent is built on a general-purpose AI model, guardrails likewise do not affect the Article 51 systemic-risk classification, which rests on high-impact capabilities assessed through appropriate technical tools, benchmarks and indicators (Article 51(1)(a)), the presumption where cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 FLOPs (Article 51(2)), or a Commission decision on the Annex XIII criteria (Article 51(1)(b)); only a genuine change in the model's capabilities or training compute bears on that threshold.
criteria_text: No - guardrails alone do not create an intermediate "moderate risk" tier; the Act's Article 6(3) derogation is binary (high-risk or exempted)

Exemption applies only where the system's intended task itself meets one of four Article 6(3) conditions: narrow procedural task; improving a previously completed human activity; detecting deviations from prior decisions without replacing human assessment; or a preparatory task
Yes - changing the system's capabilities/intended use can exit high-risk status if the redefined task now satisfies one of those conditions
Exception: an AI system that performs profiling of natural persons is always high-risk, regardless of guardrails or intended-use changes

rows.question: Is the use of deep-fake images in university classes to represent e.g. skin conditions in patients allowed? Does the artificial nature of the content need to be disclosed for such an evidently educational and illustrative use? If so, does the lighter transparency requirement apply like for certain law enforcement situations?
rows.answer: Yes, the use is allowed, but the artificial nature must be disclosed, and no lighter law‑enforcement‑style regime applies. Nothing in the cited transparency rules bars generating synthetic clinical images for teaching; Article 50 regulates how such content must be labelled, not whether it may be produced. A university (or the lecturer acting on its behalf) that uses an AI system to generate or manipulate image content constituting a deep fake is a deployer and must, under Article 50(4) first subparagraph, disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated. The educational and illustrative character of the use is not an exemption: Article 50(4) contains only two relief limbs for image, audio or video deep fakes, and neither covers teaching. The first is a genuine carve‑out, not a lighter duty: the disclosure obligation "shall not apply where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offence" (Article 50(4), second sentence). Classroom illustration of dermatological presentations is not a law‑enforcement‑authorised use, so that derogation is unavailable, and it is an all‑or‑nothing exclusion, so there is no attenuated version of it that could be borrowed by analogy. The second is the softened regime for content forming part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous work or programme, where transparency is limited to disclosing the existence of the generated or manipulated content in an appropriate manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work (Article 50(4), third subparagraph). Synthetic images presented to students as accurate depictions of real skin pathology are shown for their veridical clinical value, not as a work whose enjoyment disclosure could spoil, so they fall outside that limb; and even if a given teaching artefact were treated as analogous, disclosure of the existence of the manipulation would still be required. The separate human‑review/editorial‑responsibility exception in the fourth subparagraph concerns only AI‑generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest and cannot excuse a deep fake. Disclosure must be given to the persons concerned in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of first exposure and must conform to applicable accessibility requirements (Article 50(5)). Separately, if the university itself provides the generating system, Article 50(2) requires the outputs to be marked in a machine‑readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated, unless the system merely performs an assistive function for standard editing or does not substantially alter the deployer's input data or its semantics. These duties are without prejudice to Chapter III and to other transparency obligations under Union or national law (Article 50(6)).

rows.question: A supermarket uses an AI tool that analyzes only current-cart and checkout anomalies (no biometrics, no face recognition, no sensitive-trait inference, no cross-context social scoring) to flag transactions for optional manual bag checks by store staff. The retailer claims this is "high risk like policing", as it: resembles investigation of potentially criminal offences (theft) + evaluates or classifies persons based on observed behaviour in a way that may lead to detrimental or unfavourable treatment. Is this situation potentially high-risk?
rows.answer: No. On the facts given, this system is neither a prohibited practice under Article 5(1) nor a high-risk system, and the retailer's self-classification as "high risk like policing" is not supported by the Regulation. The policing analogy fails at the threshold: Annex III's law-enforcement area is confined to systems used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities (or Union bodies supporting them), and none of the other seven Annex III areas, biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, access to essential private and public services and benefits, law enforcement, migration/asylum/border control, administration of justice and democratic processes, covers a private retailer's own in-store loss-prevention at its own checkouts. A supermarket flagging its own transactions for an optional staff bag check is not exercising a law-enforcement function, and only a use-case actually listed in Annex III makes a system high-risk on that route; nor is the tool a safety component of a product covered by the Annex I product route. The prohibitions are equally not engaged. Article 5(1)(c) requires evaluation or classification of persons over a certain period of time based on social behaviour or known, inferred or predicted personal or personality characteristics, producing a social score that leads to detrimental or unfavourable treatment either (i) in social contexts unrelated to the context in which the data was generated or collected, or (ii) that is unjustified or disproportionate to the social behaviour or its gravity. A tool confined to the current cart and checkout anomalies builds no persistent score over time, uses no personality characteristics, and its consequence, a bag check at the same till, in the same commercial context that generated the data, is neither cross-contextual nor, on these facts, disproportionate to the conduct observed. Article 5(1)(d) prohibits risk assessments of natural persons to assess or predict the risk of committing a criminal offence based solely on profiling or on assessing personality traits and characteristics, and expressly does not apply to AI systems used to support the human assessment of a person's involvement in criminal activity where that assessment is already based on objective and verifiable facts directly linked to a criminal activity. Checkout and cart anomalies are objective, verifiable transactional facts, not profiling or personality assessment, and the output only supports a discretionary human bag check rather than producing the assessment itself, so the practice falls outside the prohibition on both counts. Two qualifications define the boundary. First, the conclusion depends on the stated facts holding in operation: no biometric processing, no inference of sensitive or personality traits, no persistent cross-visit or cross-context scoring of identified individuals, and flags used only to inform a human decision. Adding customer-identity linkage and a cumulative "suspicion score" carried across visits or shared into unrelated contexts would move the analysis toward Article 5(1)(c), and adding biometric identification or categorisation would open the Annex III biometrics area. Second, Article 5(8) preserves prohibitions arising under other Union law, so data-protection, non-discrimination and consumer-law constraints on the profiling and on discriminatory application of bag checks continue to apply independently of the AI Act classification, as does the Article 4 AI literacy duty owed by the retailer as deployer.

A supermarket's own loss-prevention/bag-check tool, run by store staff, is not used by or on behalf of a law enforcement authority, so it falls outside Annex III.6 regardless of its resemblance to investigative or evaluative functions

rows.question: We developed a product listed in Annex I where an AI system is a safety component. We had the option to opt out of the third-party conformity assessment base case by using harmonized standards. Thus no third-party conformity assessment happened. This means we can skip the requirements of Chapter 3 Section 2 of the AI Act, right?
rows.answer: No, the requirements of Chapter III, Section 2 continue to apply in full, and using the opt-out is lawful only because you also apply harmonised standards covering those requirements. The operator's system is high-risk under Article 6(1): it is intended to be used as a safety component of a product covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I (point (a)), and that product is, as a base case, required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment with a view to its placing on the market or putting into service under that legislation (point (b)). Classification turns on the product being subject to that regime, not on whether a notified body was in fact involved in the operator's individual case; electing a manufacturer's option within the sectoral act does not remove the system from the Annex I route. Article 43(3) then governs exactly the operator's situation. For high-risk AI systems covered by legislation listed in Section A of Annex I, the provider follows the relevant sectoral conformity assessment procedure, and the requirements set out in Section 2 of Chapter III apply to those systems and form part of that assessment; points 4.3., 4.4., 4.5. And the fifth paragraph of point 4.6 of Annex VII also apply. Where the sectoral act enables the product manufacturer to opt out from a third-party conformity assessment on condition that it has applied all harmonised standards covering all the relevant requirements, Article 43(3) permits use of that option only if the manufacturer has also applied harmonised standards or, where applicable, common specifications referred to in Article 41 covering all requirements set out in Section 2. The opt-out is therefore not a waiver of Section 2 but a substitution of a documented standards-based route for notified-body control: if the operator's harmonised-standards coverage does not extend to every Section 2 requirement, risk management, data and data governance, technical documentation, record-keeping, instructions for use and transparency to deployers, human oversight, and accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, the condition in Article 43(3) is not met and the opt-out was not available to you. Two consequences follow. First, absence of notified-body involvement does not reduce the operator's substantive duties; it increases the operator's evidentiary burden, since the Section 2 conformity must be demonstrable from the operator's own technical documentation and quality management system, and Annex VII points 4.3. Remain applicable to the assessment to the extent Article 43(3) makes them so. Second, under Article 43(4), a system already subject to a conformity assessment must undergo a new conformity assessment in the event of a substantial modification, regardless of whether the modified system is further distributed or continues to be used by the current deployer; pre-determined changes to a continuously learning system that were documented at the initial assessment under point 2(f) of Annex IV do not constitute a substantial modification. A modification that takes the system outside the harmonised standards you relied on would also remove the basis on which the opt-out was exercised.
